title: Symmetry Breaking by Interfacial Dead Layers: Observation of Forbidden Self-Induced Spin-Orbit Torque in Symmetric Ferromagnets
authors: Athira Ravindran K, Raghvendra Posti, Manish Kumar Mohanta, Abhishek Kumar, Damanpreet Kaur, Alberto Anadón, Sebastien Petit-Watelot, Juan-Carlos Rojas-Sánchez, Michel Hehn, Puru Jena, Debangsu Roy
abstract: Conventionally, spin-orbit torques (SOTs) in ferromagnets require heavy-metal layers or engineered structural asymmetry to break inversion symmetry. In this work, we report the observation of robust, self-generated SOTs in a nominally symmetric, heavy-metal-free MgO/NiFe/MgO trilayer - a geometry where such torques are theoretically forbidden. By combining harmonic Hall measurements with SQUID magnetometry and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, we identify the symmetry-breaking origin: a 1.8 nm magnetic dead layer at the bottom interface. Crucially, we demonstrate a quantitative agreement between our data and the drift-diffusion theory predicted by Kim and Lee, yielding a theoretically extracted dead-layer thickness (1.2 nm) which matches structural characterization. Furthermore, density-functional calculations confirm that NiFe possesses sufficient intrinsic spin Hall conductivity to support the observed spin currents. These results reframe the parasitic dead layer as a functional spintronic component, establishing a universal, all-ferromagnetic route to SOTs in standard magnetic heterostructures.
summary: This work reports observing robust Spin-Orbit Torques (SOTs) in a nominally symmetric ferromagnet ($	ext{MgO}/	ext{NiFe}/	ext{MgO}$), where they should theoretically vanish. The authors pinpoint the cause as a naturally formed magnetic dead layer at the bottom interface, demonstrating that this 'parasitic' feature can be quantified and utilized as an intrinsic source of symmetry breaking for spintronic applications.
main_problem: The study addresses how robust Spin-Orbit Torques (SOTs) can be generated in nominally symmetric ferromagnets, circumventing the conventional requirement for structural asymmetry or heavy metals.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that a naturally occurring magnetic dead layer at an interface acts as the source of symmetry breaking, enabling measurable SOTs in standard all-ferromagnetic heterostructures.
method: The research combines harmonic Hall measurements to quantify torques, SQUID magnetometry for magnetization characterization, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) depth profiling to identify the structural asymmetry.
model_or_system: The physical system is an MgO/NiFe/MgO trilayer structure. The theoretical framework involves fitting transport data using a drift-diffusion model adapted from Kim and Lee theory to quantify spin current absorption at interfaces.
key_observables: Second-harmonic Hall resistance ($R_{xy}^{2\omega}$), extracted damping-like and field-like torque effective fields ($	ext{H}_{	ext{AD},y}$, $	ext{H}_{	ext{FL},y}$), and the thickness dependence of these torques.
important_parameters: The key parameters include the thickness ($t$) of the NiFe layer, the derived dead-layer thickness ($\sim 1.2 	ext{ nm}$ vs $1.8 	ext{ nm}$ measured), and the intrinsic spin Hall conductivity ($\sigma_{xy}^z$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that by measuring angular dependence of $R_{xy}^{2\omega}$, contributions from AHE and PHE can be successfully isolated, allowing focus on spin-current related torques.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometry and magnetization curves; subsequent figures show the angular dependence of Hall resistance components separated into symmetric/antisymmetric parts, field dependence of fit coefficients, and thickness evolution of SOT effective fields.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by noting the theoretical prohibition of SOTs in symmetric structures. It then presents experimental measurements using harmonic Hall techniques to observe torques. The source is identified through XPS/SQUID analysis pointing to an interfacial dead layer, which is finally quantified by fitting transport data against theory.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the concept of emergent symmetry breaking via interface disorder or reconstruction—and quantifying this effect using advanced transport measurements—is analogous to studying boundary conditions in quantum many-body systems.
